lead: Two op-amps and a few passive parts make a square wave, a triangle wave and a sawtooth wave. A Schmitt trigger snaps between two fixed levels; an integrator turns those levels into straight ramps; the ramps come back and trip the trigger again. The loop starts by itself and needs no tuned LC circuit. Bench function generators, the ramp inside a PWM motor drive, an oscilloscope timebase and the clock of a successive-approximation ADC all use this idea. Because the frequency depends only on resistor and capacitor values, it is easy to predict and easy to set.
prereq: You need: the comparator and Schmitt trigger from Unit 6 (Op-Amp Linear and Nonlinear Applications), and the op-amp integrator from 7.3.

sections.h3: Square wave from a Schmitt trigger

blocks.text: A Schmitt trigger is a comparator with two thresholds (Unit 6). Its output cannot stop in between: it sits at +V<sub>sat</sub> or −V<sub>sat</sub>, within a volt or two of the supplies, because positive feedback drives it all the way.
R<sub>2</sub> runs from the output to the non-inverting input, and R<sub>1</sub> runs from that input to ground. The non-inverting input therefore sits at a fixed fraction of the output.

blocks.where: β is the feedback fraction (no unit); R<sub>1</sub> is the resistor from the non-inverting input to ground, in Ω; R<sub>2</sub> is the resistor from the output to the non-inverting input, in Ω; V<sub>sat</sub> is the saturated output magnitude, in V.

blocks.text: Put the integrator output on the inverting input. The integrator is non-inverting, so the ramp rises while the square is at +V<sub>sat</sub>. While the ramping voltage stays below +βV<sub>sat</sub>, the output stays at +V<sub>sat</sub>. When the ramp crosses +βV<sub>sat</sub> the comparator flips to −V<sub>sat</sub> and the threshold drops to −βV<sub>sat</sub>. The next flip needs the ramp to climb down to −βV<sub>sat</sub>. The output is a square wave whose edges are spaced by the time the ramp takes to cross between the two thresholds.

A non-inverting integrator gives vout = +(1/RC)∫vin dt, so a constant input makes a straight ramp of slope +vin/(RC). (The inverting integrator from 7.3 followed by an inverter also works.) The square wave is ±Vsat, so the slope is ±Vsat/(RC) in V/s. The sign flips at every edge, so the integrator traces up and down between the thresholds, and its peak is exactly the threshold that caused the switch, ±βVsat.
One half period is the time to travel 2βV<sub>sat</sub> at slope V<sub>sat</sub>/(RC). That time is 2βRC, so the full period is 4βRC.

blocks.where: f is the output frequency in Hz; β is the feedback fraction R<sub>1</sub>/(R<sub>1</sub> + R<sub>2</sub>); R is the integrator input resistor in Ω; C is the integrator capacitor in F.

blocks.text: V<sub>sat</sub> cancels. The ramp slope and the thresholds both scale with the supply, so supply drift leaves the frequency alone; only β, R and C set it.

The triangle peak lines up with a square edge. When the ramp reaches +βV<sub>sat</sub>, the square has just fallen to −V<sub>sat</sub>; when the ramp reaches −βV<sub>sat</sub>, the square has just risen to +V<sub>sat</sub>. Sketch the square on top and the triangle below, and every corner of the triangle sits under a transition of the square. The two slopes are equal, so the duty cycle is exactly 50 %.

A sawtooth has unequal rise and fall. The capacitor must charge through one resistance and discharge through another. Split the integrator input resistor into R<sub>A</sub> and R<sub>B</sub>, each in series with a diode pointing opposite ways. The diode that conducts while the square is at +V<sub>sat</sub> sets the rising-path resistance R<sub>A</sub>. The other diode, which conducts while the square is at −V<sub>sat</sub>, sets the falling-path resistance R<sub>B</sub>.

blocks.where: duty is the fraction of the period spent rising; R<sub>A</sub> is the resistance on the rising path in Ω; R<sub>B</sub> is the resistance on the falling path in Ω; β, C as before.

blocks.text: If a potentiometer splits one fixed resistance, the total R<sub>A</sub> + R<sub>B</sub> stays constant. The duty knob then moves the duty cycle and leaves the frequency almost unchanged. With R<sub>A</sub> = 5 kΩ rising and R<sub>B</sub> = 20 kΩ falling, the duty cycle is 20 %.

A single op-amp relaxation oscillator needs no separate integrator: the capacitor charges straight from the output, so the ramps are exponential and T = 2RC ln((1+β)/(1−β)). The 555 timer charges one capacitor between two fixed fractions of the supply in the same way (7.6). Exponential ramps are cheap; a straight ramp from an integrator is used when the sawtooth must be linear, as in a timebase or a PWM ramp.

figure.caption: The Schmitt trigger gives the square wave and the integrator turns it into a triangle that comes back to switch the trigger. With β = 1/3, R = 10 kΩ and C = 10 nF the loop runs at 7.5 kHz with thresholds at ±4 V.

spec.aria: A Schmitt trigger with thresholds at plus and minus beta times V_sat feeding a square output, and an integrator with R and C producing a triangle that is fed back to the trigger.

examples.question: A function generator is built from a Schmitt trigger and an integrator. The Schmitt trigger runs on ±12 V supplies and saturates at ±12 V. R<sub>1</sub> = 10 kΩ goes from the non-inverting input to ground and R<sub>2</sub> = 20 kΩ goes from the output to that input. The integrator uses R = 10 kΩ and C = 10 nF. Find (a) β and the thresholds, (b) the frequency, (c) the triangle amplitude peak-to-peak, (d) the ramp slope and the half period, and (e) check whether an op-amp with 0.5 V/µs slew rate is fast enough.
steps: Feedback fraction: β = R<sub>1</sub>/(R<sub>1</sub> + R<sub>2</sub>) = 10 kΩ/(10 kΩ + 20 kΩ) = 1/3 = 0.3333.
Thresholds: ±βV<sub>sat</sub> = ±0.3333 × 12 V = ±4 V. The triangle swings from −4 V to +4 V.
Integrator time constant: RC = 10 kΩ × 10 nF = 10 × 10³ × 10 × 10⁻⁹ s = 100 µs.
Ramp slope: V<sub>sat</sub>/(RC) = 12 V/100 µs = 0.12 V/µs = 1.2 × 10⁵ V/s.
Half period: the ramp travels 8 V at 0.12 V/µs, so T/2 = 8 V ÷ 0.12 V/µs = 66.7 µs and T = 133.3 µs. Then 1/T = 7.5 kHz, which matches step 5.
Slew-rate check: the op-amp must follow 0.12 V/µs. With 0.5 V/µs available the margin is about 4 times, so the triangle stays straight at this frequency.
examples.answer: β = 1/3, thresholds ±4 V, f = 7.5 kHz, triangle ±4 V (8 V peak-to-peak), slope 0.12 V/µs, half period 66.7 µs; a 0.5 V/µs op-amp is fast enough.
examples.check:
R1=10e3
R2=20e3
R=10e3
C=10e-9
Vsat=12.0
beta=R1/(R1+R2)
print(round(beta,4))
print(round(beta*Vsat,4))
print(round(1/(4*beta*R*C),4))
slope=Vsat/(R*C)
print(round(slope,4))
t_half=(2*beta*Vsat)/slope
print(round(t_half*1e6,4))

traps: Swapping the outputs: the square wave comes from the Schmitt trigger and the triangle from the integrator. Labelling them the other way loses the marks for the whole sketch.
Dropping β: f = 1/(2RC) or 1/(2πRC) is wrong here. The threshold fraction must appear as f = 1/(4βRC).
Reading amplitude as peak-to-peak: the triangle swings ±βV<sub>sat</sub>, so its peak-to-peak value is 2βV<sub>sat</sub>. Answer whichever the question asks.
Expecting the supply to set the frequency: V<sub>sat</sub> cancels out. Changing the supply moves the amplitude and the slope, not f (to first order).
Assuming every duty control keeps f fixed: diode steering changes f as duty changes, while a potentiometer across a fixed total resistance keeps f nearly constant. State which one the circuit uses.

quiz.q: What are the two thresholds of the Schmitt trigger in this loop, in terms of the resistors?
quiz.a: ±βV<sub>sat</sub>, with β = R<sub>1</sub>/(R<sub>1</sub> + R<sub>2</sub>), where R<sub>1</sub> goes from the non-inverting input to ground and R<sub>2</sub> from the output to that input.

quiz.q: Why does the oscillation frequency not depend on V<sub>sat</sub>?
quiz.a: The ramp slope is proportional to V<sub>sat</sub> and the distance to be travelled, 2βV<sub>sat</sub>, is also proportional to it. In T/2 = 2βV<sub>sat</sub> × RC/V<sub>sat</sub> the supply cancels, leaving T = 4βRC.

quiz.q: At the instant the triangle reaches +βV<sub>sat</sub>, what is the state of the square output?
quiz.a: It has just switched to −V<sub>sat</sub>. The triangle peak coincides with a square edge, because the crossing is what causes the switch.

quiz.q: A Schmitt-trigger and integrator loop has β = 1/4, R = 20 kΩ and C = 1 nF. Find the frequency.
The same loop saturates at ±9 V and has β = 0.4. Give the thresholds and the peak-to-peak triangle amplitude.
quiz.a: Thresholds ±βV<sub>sat</sub> = ±0.4 × 9 V = ±3.6 V. Peak-to-peak = 2 × 3.6 V = 7.2 V.

quiz.q: A sawtooth generator uses diode paths with R<sub>A</sub> = 5 kΩ on the rising path and R<sub>B</sub> = 20 kΩ on the falling path, β = 1/3 and C = 10 nF. Find the duty cycle and the frequency.
quiz.a: Duty = R<sub>A</sub>/(R<sub>A</sub> + R<sub>B</sub>) = 5/25 = 0.2, that is 20 %. Total resistance 25 kΩ, so T = 2βC(R<sub>A</sub> + R<sub>B</sub>) = 2 × 0.3333 × 10 nF × 25 kΩ = 1.6667 × 10⁻⁴ s, giving f = 6 kHz.

quiz.q: You want to raise the frequency of the square-triangle loop without changing the triangle amplitude. Which component do you change, and which must you leave alone?
quiz.a: Change R or C in the integrator: f = 1/(4βRC) moves while the amplitude ±βV<sub>sat</sub> stays fixed. Do not change R<sub>1</sub> or R<sub>2</sub>, because β sets the amplitude as well as the frequency.

beyond: Not for the exam. Monolithic function-generator ICs put a current-steering integrator, a comparator with hysteresis and a sine shaper on one chip, so square, triangle and sine come from the same core. In CMOS design a current-starved ring oscillator replaces the Schmitt-and-integrator loop, but the same trade appears: RC accuracy against wide current tuning. The ramp that a switching power supply compares against its error voltage is this circuit, and so is the timebase sweep of an analog oscilloscope. Search for 'function generator IC', 'current-starved ring oscillator' and 'PWM ramp generator' to go further.
